event_description: Determination of a State of Emergency in Tillamook County due to Heavy Rain and Flooding
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several days of nearly non-stop weather systems brought copious amounts of rainfall to northwest Oregon.  With moderate temperatures in place, very close to all of this rainfall became run-off, and many rivers over the area swelled in response.  Many rivers reached and maintained flood stage for a couple days.  |One river in particular, the Wilson River near Tillamook, recorded record flooding.  This river's flood stage is 12.0 feet, and the river crested at 22.8 feet (38,500 cfs), well above major flood stage.  The town of Tillamook, downstream from this gauge, was underwater for several days after the crest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Clackamas River near Estacada crested at 22.3 feet on November 7th, with flood stage at 20.0 feet.

event_description: Determination of State of Emergency in Oregon Due to a Severe Winter Storm that Includes High Winds, Flooding, and Landslides
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two very powerful storms with origins in the Tropics brought hazardous weather to the Pacific Northwest. The entire forecast area experienced heavy rainfall for an extended period of time. As an example of the extreme accumulations, over fourteen inches of rain fell at Lees Camp in the north Coast Range in a period of about 60 hours. This abnormally long period of consistently heavy rainfall led to widespread flooding, with the worst hit areas in the Coast Range and areas draining from the Coast Range to the Pacific Ocean. Five rivers in northwest Oregon surpassed major flood stages, fueling the extensive flood damage across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Marys River flooded near Philomath, causing extensive flooding and flood damage in the city of Philomath and surrounding areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On September 16, unusually hot and dry conditions coupled with a persistent thermal belt during the night caused the persistent Gnarl Ridge Fire to make a major run shortly after midnight. event_description: Invocation of Emergency Conflagration Act for the Siskiyou Fire in Jackson County
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two wildfires developed in southern Jackson county on 09/21/09.  The first was the Siskiyou fire, which developed south of Ashland in the morning.  In the afternoon, the Deer Ridge fire started on the east edge of Medford. Occasional gusts meeting warning criteria continued until 19/1838 PST.  The Rock Creek RAWS reported gusts exceeding 57 mph over a much smaller span...18/0627 PST until 18/1127 PST.  The peak gust was 65 mph at 18/1127 PST.  The Summit RAWS reported gusts exceeding 57 mph in several stretches between 18/0503 PST and 19/1203 PST.  The peak gust was 71 mph at 18/1003 PST.  The Coffee Pot RAWS had one gust to 63 mph at 19/1044 PST.  Many spotter reports were also received.  A spotter 9SSE Summer Lake reported a gust to 64 mph at 17/2112 PST, a gust to 72 mph at 18/0740 PST with tree damage and power outages, a gust to 81 mph at 18/0855 PST with blizzard conditions in blowing snow as well as damage to a hay farm and carport, gusts to 65 mph at 19/0000 and a semi-trailer blown off the road at milepost 92 on Highway 31.  A spotter 2NE Valley Falls reported a gust to 69 mph at 18/0558 PST, a gust to 76 mph at 18/1000 PST, and a gust to 77 mph at 19/1246 PST.  A spotter SSW Silver Lake reported a gust to 70 mph at 18/0924 PST.  A member of the public reported a gust to 88 mph at 19/1003 PST with roof damage.  An emergency manager in Summer Lake reported a gust to 71 mph at 19/1128 PST with roof damage at 17 homes in Ana Estates and overturned irrigation pivots.

event_description: Invocation of Emergency Conflagration Act for the Two Bulls Wildfire in Deschutes County
CZ_NAME: EAST SLOPES OF THE OREGON CASCADES
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Oregon Department of Forestry's Incident Management Team 2 (Incident Commander Chris Cline) and the Oregon State Fire Marshal's Office Incident Management Team Green (Incident Commander John Ingrao) were dispatched to and assumed joint incident command at noon on Sunday, June 8, 2014, of the Two Bulls Fires. These two fires, burning towards each other when first reported (Saturday afternoon, June 7), are being managed as one incident, are located approximately 10 miles northwest of Bend, and burning in a mix of Deschutes National Forest and private lands protected by the Oregon Department of Forestry. The wind- and terrain-driven fires prompted immediate evacuations in areas west of Bend, as well as additional threats/evacuation notices. Evacuations and the threats to structures were downgraded within a few days, with the Oregon State Fire Marshal's Office Incident Management Team Green demobilized at the end of shift on June 10. On Saturday, June 14, 2014, responsibility for management of the Two Bulls Fire transitioned to a local Type 3 fire team. At the time of transition, no homes or structures had been damaged or lost as a result of this fire, however, the fire burned approximately 6,908 acres of public and private forestlands.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: InciWeb Report.

event_description: Invocation of Emergency Conflagration Act for the Beachie Creek and Lionshead Fires in Marion County
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a period of upper level ridging brought a return to above normal temperatures in early September, very strong easterly downslope and offshore winds off the Cascades and Coastal Ranges occurred. Winds increased rapidly during the afternoon and evening of September 7 with the passage of an unseasonably strong backdoor cold front, and persisted through much of the following day. This resulted in extremely critical fire weather conditions when the strong winds combined with extremely low relative humidity and exceptionally dry existing fuel conditions. The result was explosive growth of ongoing wildfires, and the new start and explosive spread of numerous new wildfires. Widespread wind gusts from 50-70 mph were common on ridge tops and numerous other in exposed areas, including portions of the greater Portland metro area, the Willamette Valley, and areas of the Oregon coast.  Strong winds caused widespread damage to trees, and downed numerous power lines across the region, which started at least 13 additional wildfires.  Large portions of the cities of Detroit, Mehama, and Gates were destroyed, and significant portions of Idanha, Mill City, and Lyons also burned. Resultant large wildfires included these named incidents - In Oregon: Beachie Creek, Chehalem Mountain/Bald Peak, Riverside, and Lionshead, and in Washington: Big Hollow. Rapidly spreading wildfires resulted in multiple fatalities, hundreds of displaced persons for many weeks, and billions of dollars in damage.

event_description: Invocation of Emergency Conflagration Act for the Beachie Creek and Lionshead Fires in Marion County
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a period of upper level ridging brought a return to above normal temperatures in early September, very strong easterly downslope and offshore winds off the Cascades and Coastal Ranges occurred. Winds increased rapidly during the afternoon and evening of September 7 with the passage of an unseasonably strong backdoor cold front, and persisted through much of the following day. This resulted in extremely critical fire weather conditions when the strong winds combined with extremely low relative humidity and exceptionally dry existing fuel conditions. The result was explosive growth of ongoing wildfires, and the new start and explosive spread of numerous new wildfires. Widespread wind gusts from 50-70 mph were common on ridge tops and numerous other in exposed areas, including portions of the greater Portland metro area, the Willamette Valley, and areas of the Oregon coast. Strong winds caused widespread damage to trees, and downed numerous power lines across the region, which started at least 13 additional wildfires. Large portions of the cities of Detroit, Mehama, and Gates were destroyed, and significant portions of Idanha, Mill City, and Lyons also burned. Resultant large wildfires included these named incidents - In Oregon: Beachie Creek, Chehalem Mountain/Bald Peak, Riverside, and Lionshead, and in Washington: Big Hollow. Rapidly spreading wildfires resulted in multiple fatalities, hundreds of displaced persons for many weeks, and billions of dollars in damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Beachie Creek wildfire started around 1100PDT on August 16, 2020 in Marion county, OR at coordinates 44.821, -122.188. The fire grew to approximately 193,500 acres before being declared officially under control on December 2, 2020. Destroyed were 486 residential homes, 36 non-residential commercial properties, 801 other minor structures. There were 160 structures damaged. Affected were the towns of Mill City, Gates, Lyons and Detroit. During this conflagration 33388 people were evacuated, 5 citizens were fatally injured; and 2 citizens and 8 responders were injured. The cause of the fire is unknown.

This resulted in extremely critical fire weather conditions when the strong winds combined with extremely low relative humidity and exceptionally dry existing fuel conditions. The result was explosive growth of ongoing wildfires, and the new start and explosive spread of numerous new wildfires. Widespread wind gusts from 50-70 mph were common on ridge tops and numerous other in exposed areas, including portions of the greater Portland metro area, the Willamette Valley, and areas of the Oregon coast. Large portions of the cities of Detroit, Mehama, and Gates were destroyed, and significant portions of Idanha, Mill City, and Lyons also burned. event_description: Declaration of State of Emergency in Harney County due to Flooding
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Flooding caused by rapid snowmelt in March continued through mid-April. The Silvies river rose to 14.76 feet, about half a foot under the record of 15.2 feet, on March 29th. The water levels began to decrease, although the area remained inundated. Another warm period in mid-April allowed for the river level to begin rising again. Reaching a secondary peak of 12.58 feet on April 11th. Water dropped below flood stage on April 15th. Flood impacts were observed through mid-late April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hundreds of homes were impacted by flood waters, many with major damage and some were uninhabitable. Numerous residents were evacuated during the height of the flooding with some sheltering in hotels and Red Cross mass care facilities. Extensive damage to sewer system.
